content: Studies comparing resistance training and aerobic exercise training have been conducted, but the evidence is often of very low certainty due to various limitations. These limitations include serious indirectness, which refers to the use of intermediate or indirect outcomes, as well as heterogeneity in exposures and comparisons. Certainty of evidence was not always downgraded for indirectness if it was judged not to impact the findings' reliability for the evaluated outcomes. However, in cases where indirectness was significant, the certainty of evidence was downgraded. Certainty of evidence was also downgraded in cases of serious imprecision in study-specific and pooled effect estimates, as well as when there was evidence of inconsistency in the range or direction of effects. In some cases, the certainty of evidence was upgraded if the body of evidence had no major limitations, even if small study effects were present. However, when serious inconsistency in the direction of effects, imprecision in effect estimates, or small study effects were observed, the certainty of evidence was downgraded. For cognitive function outcomes, the association between physical activity and cognitive measures in adults has been explored. For example, two cross-sectional studies among older adults (mean ages 64 and 65 years) examined light physical activity (LPA). One study found a significant association between LPA and higher cognitive functioning, while the other found no association with spatial working memory or task-switching. The certainty of evidence for these findings was rated as very low. In another study, multicomponent physical activity interventions (including flexibility, strength, balance, endurance, and aerobic training) were tested in four trials involving older adults aged over 60 years without cognitive impairment. These trials primarily included white women. A wide range of neuropsychological tests were used to assess cognitive function, but only 3 out of 25 comparisons showed statistically significant benefits of multicomponent physical activity interventions compared to attention controls. One trial reported no difference in the incidence of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or dementia between groups after two years. The certainty of evidence for these findings was rated as low. Aerobic training was tested in six trials among healthy older adults. One study found that participants in the aerobic exercise group were significantly less likely to receive a dementia diagnosis at 18 months. However, only 11 out of 35 comparisons showed statistically significant benefits on cognitive function measures, while 24 comparisons showed no significant differences between groups. The certainty of evidence for these findings was rated as low. Resistance training was examined in three trials among frail older adults. None of these trials reported diagnostic outcomes, and less than one-third of comparisons favored the intervention for measures of executive function, attention, processing speed, and memory. The certainty of evidence for these findings was rated as very low. A small trial tested Tai Chi versus attention control in older adults aged 60–79 years. Only one out of two outcomes for executive function, attention, and processing speed showed a significant benefit. The certainty of evidence for these findings was rated as low. A systematic review of studies evaluating the relationship between physical activity interventions and cognitive function among adults aged 50 years and older found that interventions such as aerobic exercise, resistance training, multicomponent training, Tai Chi, and yoga had varying effects. A multi-level analysis combining multiple measures of cognitive performance per study found a significant effect of physical activity interventions compared to no activity. However, the certainty of evidence was rated as moderate due to serious risk of bias, inconsistency, and indirectness. Another systematic review focused on working memory performance and found that 10 out of 15 studies reported statistically significant improvements in working memory among participants in physical activity interventions compared to no activity. However, no association was found between acute physical activity interventions and working memory performance. The certainty of evidence for these findings was rated as low. Exergames, which combine physical activity with gaming, were found to significantly improve global cognitive function in older adults. Statistically significant effects were also observed for specific cognitive domains such as executive function, task-switching, inhibitory control, and attentional processing speed. However, no significant effects were found for working memory, reasoning, verbal learning and memory, spatial learning and memory, or language. The certainty of evidence for these findings was rated as very low. The methodological quality of systematic reviews included in this analysis was assessed using the AMSTAR 2 tool, which evaluates the reliability of systematic reviews. Reviews with critical methodological flaws were excluded to ensure the accuracy of the evidence summary. The overall certainty of evidence for the included studies varied, with many findings rated as low or very low due to limitations such as risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, and imprecision.
